blocks.text: What Joel says about locusts in his first chapter.

So far concerning the Egyptian locusts. With locusts like these the prophet Joel threatened the Israelites in the gravest terms, but at last he ends in words of peace and in God's name promises them many good things. It is therefore our task to pick out from Joel whatever he says about locusts and to interpret it as best we can, as each passage occurs and keeping to the Prophet's order. To capture attention, he declares at the very outset that he is about to say things new and unheard of, ch. I, 2: Hear this, he says, you old men, and give ear, all you inhabitants of the land: Has this happened in your days, or in the days of your fathers? First he addresses the old men, who by the benefit of age had seen and heard more. So Moses, Deut. XXXII, 7: Ask the old men, and they will tell you. And Job XXXII, 7: Days will speak, and the multitude of years will teach wisdom. The Prophet therefore signifies that the locusts of which he is about to speak wrought such destruction as none recorded in any age. In Judaea, that is. For this is the point of Hear this, you old men; and give ear, all you inhabitants of the land: supply [col. 465] of Judaea, which is the subject here. Likewise, when we read of the Egyptians in Exod. X, 14, Before them there were no such locusts as these, nor shall there be after them, this must be restricted to Egypt. Otherwise Moses would conflict with Joel, or Joel with Moses. For the other explanations which the Hebrews offer are less to the point, as we shall show below.
In the third verse, Tell this to your children, and your children to their children, and their children to another generation] Which you might express in the words of the Poet:
And the children's children, and those who shall be born of them.

For God's remarkable deeds must not be buried in oblivion; their memory must be diligently passed on to posterity and preserved for the future. Thus we may either be grateful and full of confidence for benefits received, or more fearful and cautious because of punishments inflicted. Hence David, Psal. LXXVIII, 3. etc.: What we have heard and known, and our fathers have told us, we will not hide from their children, another generation, so that they may tell the praises of the Lord, and his might, and the wonders that he has done, etc. And he commanded our fathers to make them known to their children, so that another generation might know, the children yet to be born, and that they might arise and tell them to their children. And that they might set their hope in God, and not forget the works of God, etc. See also Deut. IV, 9. and VI, 6. 20. Ios. IV, 6. etc.
